rv.q: If this isn't great acting, I don't know what is.
...it’s a terrific take on one of the greatest plays ever written
To see a mighty actor at the peak of his power in his 80s, and a younger one beginning to soar.

At 84, there’s clearly life in the acting titan yet (and long may it be). Even so, an unmistakable aura of elegy and mortality hangs over his largely delightful and affecting turn as old Jack Falstaff, who, with his shaggy beard and wispy white hair, inevitably recalls Gandalf but has a gargantuan belly and little of the wizard’s wisdom.
Sir Ian McKellen's considerable charisma almost single-handedly sustains this always challenging play as Falstaff japes on alone and Hal is drawn into the orbit of his ailing father.
There is no doubting that Player Kings, Robert Icke's adaptation of Shakespeare's Henry IV Parts 1 & 2 (and a sliver of Henry V) is McKellen's show.
Overall there's a piercing, vivid immediacy to Icke's staging.
Robert Icke has taken Shakespeare's two Henry IV plays and fused them into an epic thriller that looks set to be this year's boldest West End hit.

Not only it is a fresh new Shakespeare production but also Ian McKellen is starring at Sir John Falstaff. Nearing four hours including the interval, this is not your typical West End show. Yet it tackles a lot of original material, combining two famous plays by Shakespeare into one complex and comprehensive production.
Player Kings, Icke's new version of Henry IV, Parts 1 and 2, is a dazzling piece of entertainment.
Player Kings certainly sets a high bar for those that follow.
His iconoclastic vision retains heart clenching bite in its subtle but salty interrogation of power.
